e.t: Ageaddair is a proper name, rendered as “Ageaddair” and also identified as “Ayeathther.” It refers to a person named in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, at 1 Chronicles 4:14. Its precise significance as a personal name cannot be established from the available lexical information, so it should be read as a name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

Adin is a proper name, also rendered Athin. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in Ezra—once in Ezra 2:15 and again in Ezra 8:6. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself gives no further meaning beyond identifying the individual called Adin or Athin.

This adjective describes someone as “bearing away the prize” or “victorious.” It presents victory as both winning and receiving the reward, so it can identify a person who has overcome and gained the prize. Within this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its central idea is triumph, with attention not only to victory itself but also to the prize that comes with it.

“Eternity” refers to unending duration—existence without a defined end. As a noun, this word names that enduring reality rather than describing an action or a temporary period. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 2:23. Its basic meaning is clear, while the precise force of the reference belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. It points to what continues without end.

This adjective describes something free from waves and therefore calm or still. It presents quietness rather than disturbance, especially in language connected with water or a peaceful condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 3:13. The word’s central idea remains simple: no waves, agitation, or tumult. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing being described.

The word refers to “sheminith” and is defined as “eighth.” It is a noun in the Greek Old Testament and appears once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 15:21. Because the available information gives no verse text or surrounding context, the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be stated more specifically. Its basic meaning remains the designation “sheminith” or “eighth.”

This adjective means “undefiled”: kept clean, pure, and free from moral or ceremonial corruption. It describes a person or thing considered untainted rather than polluted or spoiled. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:22, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word functions as a description, attributing purity to whatever it modifies.

Anameel is a proper name, rendered as “Anameēl” or “Anamil.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs five times, all in Jeremiah, from Jeremiah 38:38 through Jeremiah 39:12. The name itself does not provide a general definition beyond identifying the individual who bears it; its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and passage. The spelling “Anamil” is another rendering of the same personal name.

This LXX noun refers to the east or to something springing up. It can name the direction associated with the rising sun, or describe emergence and growth. The word occurs seven times in the LXX corpus, across six Old Testament verses and one Deuterocanonical verse. Its precise sense in any particular passage depends on whether the surrounding sentence points to a direction or to something coming forth.

This LXX Greek verb means to set something or someone against another, or to oppose. It describes active resistance or placing in opposition rather than simple difference. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings represented here: once in Leviticus and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains opposition or deliberate resistance.

This adjective means “invisible”: not seen by the eyes or not visible to ordinary human sight. It describes something that cannot be observed directly, rather than naming an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, including Genesis 1:2, Isaiah 45:3, and 2 Maccabees 9:5. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is described as invisible, but the word itself consistently points to what is unseen or beyond visible perception.

This Greek word means “toss away”: to throw something aside or cast it off rather than keep or retain it. It is a verb, so it describes an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 41 times, showing repeated use for the act of sending something away. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This word is a proper name, represented in English as “Hasebeias” or “Asevias.” It functions as a name rather than as an ordinary description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 21 times, including passages in Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, with two additional occurrences in the deuterocanonical books. The surrounding verse is needed to identify whom or what the name denotes.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Achiloud” or “Akhiluth.” It identifies a particular person or name-bearing figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 18:15. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, the name’s specific identity cannot be explained further here; its lexical function is simply to designate an individual by name.

Achipha, also rendered Akhifa, is a personal name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition, and its meaning is presented as the name itself rather than as a translated quality or action. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nehemiah 7:53. Without the surrounding verse text, the name alone does not establish anything further about the person or the role associated with him.

This word is a proper name, identifying the named place or entity called “Baithēl” or “Vethil.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general object; it functions as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs 64 times in the LXX corpus, beginning in Genesis 12:8 and appearing repeatedly through the Old Testament, including Genesis, Joshua, and Judges. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Beniamin, also rendered Veniamin, is a proper name. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies the biblical name Beniamin rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs 177 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical material, beginning in Genesis and continuing through later books. Its exact reference—whether to the person, his descendants, or the tribe associated with him—depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name rendered as “Bōrazē” or “Vorazi.” It identifies a named person or figure rather than describing an action, characteristic, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Esther 1:10, and no broader lexical meaning is given here beyond the name itself. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage.

Gamariou is a proper name identifying a person, not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its recorded meaning is the name itself: “Gamariou,” also rendered in the lexical entry as “Gamariu.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Jeremiah. Because the available information does not provide the surrounding verse text, this entry identifies the name but does not establish the person’s role or significance in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “sweeten”: it describes making something sweet or causing it to become sweet. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, occurring 13 times across 13 verses. The word appears in Exodus, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Sirach, showing that its basic sense is an action involving sweetness rather than a person, object, or abstract title. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Gomorra is a proper name for a place known in the Old Testament. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 20 times across 20 verses, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Zephaniah. It is especially frequent in Genesis, where the name first appears, and it also occurs in later prophetic books. The word itself identifies the place; its particular significance in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Danitōn; Thaniton.” It identifies a particular named subject in the Greek LXX, rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Chronicles 12:36. The available lexical information does not specify more about the name’s referent, so its precise significance depends on the surrounding passage. Its main function is to name, not to describe.

This word means “afraid”: it describes being frightened or fearful. As a verb, it expresses the experience of becoming or being afraid rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the expression of fear or apprehension.

“Break in twain” means to split or break something into two parts. It is a verb describing an action of dividing something by breaking it, rather than merely moving or separating it. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs once, in Lamentations 4:4. The reference identifies its only recorded occurrence, but the word’s basic lexical sense remains the act of breaking something in two. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “make very wide” or “dilate,” describing the act of enlarging or spreading something so that it has greater breadth. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezekiel 41:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and architectural context, but its basic sense is to make something broader or more spacious.

This noun means “preservation” or “reserve”: something kept safe, retained, or set apart for continued use. It describes the act or result of holding something in protection rather than allowing it to be lost or consumed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Exodus and Numbers, where its recurring sense concerns something being carefully kept or held in reserve. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea is guarded preservation.

This word refers to justice—the quality or principle of what is right and fair. It is a noun, so it names this idea rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 12 times, showing that it is used across several settings while retaining its central sense of justice. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

“Guard kept over” refers to a watch or protective guard maintained over someone or something. It is a noun describing the duty or arrangement of keeping watch, rather than the person who performs it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 3:28. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is an established protective watch.

Ezekia is a proper name—the Greek LXX form of a person’s name. It refers to named individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In this LXX corpus, it appears 13 times, all within Old Testament verses, including accounts connected with the historical king Hezekiah and other family or personal references. The name is found in 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, and Nehemiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

This verb means to “intrude” or “travel into,” describing movement into a place or area, sometimes with the sense of entering where access or boundaries matter. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 150 times, showing that it is a regularly used word for entering or moving in. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek verb means “escape”: to get away from danger, capture, harm, or an unwanted situation. It describes the act of fleeing or successfully getting free rather than remaining trapped or exposed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 19 times, including passages from Judges, Proverbs, Isaiah, and several later books. The surrounding verse determines whether the escape is physical, figurative, sudden, or sought as a form of safety.

This adjective means “ivory” and describes something associated with or made of ivory. It identifies ivory as the relevant material or quality rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times across 10 verses, showing a specific but recurring material description. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the noun or object it describes.

The word is the proper name “Hellenismos; Ellinizmos,” a transliterated designation rather than an English description. In the Greek LXX corpus represented by this entry, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 4:13. Its precise sense in that passage depends on the verse and surrounding context, which are not provided here. The term should therefore be preserved as a named expression without adding an unsupported meaning or interpretation.

This verb means “change completely,” describing a thorough alteration rather than a minor adjustment. It presents something as becoming different in a significant or total way. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Genesis and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains complete change or transformation.

This verb means to display or show something, making it visible or bringing it before others. It can describe an action in which a person presents, points out, or demonstrates something rather than keeping it hidden. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 12 times, so its central sense is consistent across several books. The exact force in any verse depends on what is being shown and to whom it is presented.

This verb means to gather—to collect something together. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Lamentations, so its normal sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word describes an act of bringing things together rather than a person, place, or abstract quality. Its precise force in any one occurrence depends on what is being gathered in that passage.

This word means “eyewitness”: a person who has personally seen something and can testify to what was observed. It is a noun naming such a witness, rather than describing an event or an act of seeing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs four times: once in Esther and three times in 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “hate”: to hold strong hostility toward someone or something. It describes an active attitude or response rather than merely noticing a difference or feeling mild dislike. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 12 times, including passages in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and situation, but its central meaning remains opposition expressed as hatred.

This word is a proper name rendered “Zabadaioi” or “Zavathei.” It identifies a named person, family, group, or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Maccabees 12:31. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the name’s precise referent cannot be identified further from this word alone.

Zabadias, also rendered Zavathias, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies one individual in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in the corpus, in 1 Chronicles 26:2. Because it is a proper name, its meaning for readers is chiefly identification: it tells us which person is being mentioned. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s particular role or significance there.

This word means “zealot”: a person marked by strong zeal, devoted commitment, or intense enthusiasm. It can also function as an adjective describing someone or something characterized by that zeal. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times, in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Nahum. Its repeated use in passages about God’s jealousy and exclusive devotion shows that the word is connected with fervent, undivided commitment, though the precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

This word is the proper name “Thaglathphalnasar,” also written “Thaglathfalnasar.” It identifies a specific person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 5:6 and 1 Chronicles 5:26. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identity, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in either passage.

This verb means to treat someone or something wonderfully, or to magnify it—to regard or present it as remarkable and worthy of honor. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, all in eight Old Testament verses, with most occurrences in Psalms. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea is extraordinary treatment or exaltation rather than ordinary action.

This word refers to a “breach” or “bruise,” naming damage caused by breaking or injury. It is a noun, so it identifies the resulting condition rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Amos 6:11. Its basic sense remains focused on a damaged place or injured area; the surrounding verse determines the specific force of the word there.

This word is a proper name for “Idoumaios,” also given as “Ithumeos.” It identifies a people-name or personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, it occurs 13 times, from Deuteronomy through 2 Maccabees. Its exact reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Iechonia-asir is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, at 1 Chronicles 3:17. The form is presented as a name in its own right, so its ordinary meaning is the person it names, not a separate concept that can be explained through a common noun or verb. The surrounding verse would be needed to say more about this individual or the name’s role in that genealogy.

This word is a proper name referring to Jonah, the person whose name appears throughout the Greek Septuagint text of the book of Jonah. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies an individual. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, all within Jonah, from Jonah 1:3 through Jonah 4:6. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name Jonah.

This Greek LXX verb means “interweave in” or “weave into.” It describes the action of incorporating one thing into another by weaving, rather than simply placing it beside it. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Exodus 28:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is the deliberate weaving of something into a larger woven work.

This word is a proper name rendered “Karmēlos” or “Karmilos.” It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 18 times across 17 verses, from Joshua through Song of Songs. Its exact referent in any particular passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text, since the name itself supplies identification rather than a broader definition.

This verb means “measure out to,” describing the act of determining or assigning a boundary, distance, or portion. It is used in the Greek Old Testament for carefully marking out land or territory, including measurements connected with Israel’s borders and allotted portions. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Numbers and Ezekiel, with additional occurrences in Amos and Micah. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being measured or assigned there.

This verb means “pour,” describing the act of causing a liquid or other flowing substance to stream out or over something. It presents pouring as an action rather than naming the substance being poured. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:2. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the deliberate act of pouring or letting something flow.

This verb means to afflict someone grievously or make that person bitter. It describes severe emotional or personal distress rather than a mild irritation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Exodus and once in Ezekiel, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. English renderings may express the idea as being embittered, but the central meaning remains intense affliction that causes deep bitterness or anguish.

Kedma is a proper name, rendered “Kedma” and also identified as “Kethma.” It refers to a person named in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name appears twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Genesis 25:15 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:31. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide a separate word-definition or verse text, its meaning is best stated as the personal name Kedma rather than assigned an additional symbolic sense.

This adjective describes something as having a tail that has been shortened or cut off. Its plain meaning is “with a docked tail,” referring to a physical condition rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 22:23. The surrounding verse determines how that description functions in its immediate setting, but the word itself identifies an animal or creature marked by a shortened tail.

This adjective means “superior”: better, higher, or more excellent than something else. It describes comparative worth or standing rather than naming a person or object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 51 times, with especially frequent use in Proverbs. Its exact force depends on what two things are being compared, but the central idea remains that one is greater or preferable to another.

This proper name refers to “Lydda,” also known as “Liththa,” a place name rather than a description or action. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 11:34. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name itself can be explained only as the designation of that place. Its role in the passage depends on how the surrounding sentence refers to Lydda.

This LXX Greek verb means “patient.” It describes acting with patience or maintaining patience, so the word presents patience as something a person does rather than simply a quality someone possesses. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books represented here, it occurs seven times, including uses in Job, Proverbs, Sirach, and Baruch. The same basic meaning remains the safest understanding wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines what situation calls for such patience.

This noun describes someone who is “vain-minded” or “weak-minded”—a person whose thinking is marked by vanity or weakness. It presents a description of the person rather than an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:11. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning points to deficient or misguided thought.

This Greek LXX verb means “middle,” expressing something as being in the middle or at a midpoint. It describes position within an interval or between two points rather than naming an object or person. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical books, including Exodus, Jeremiah, and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun means “womb,” the place within a woman where a child develops before birth. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it refers to the mother’s womb in discussions of conception, birth, and the firstborn. The word occurs 31 times in this LXX corpus, with uses ranging from Genesis through Sirach. Its basic meaning remains the bodily womb; the surrounding verse determines the particular point being made about it.

This noun means “red chalk” or “ruddle,” a red mineral pigment used as a coloring material. It names a physical substance rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs two times: once in Jeremiah and once in Wisdom. The precise significance of the substance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary meaning remains a red coloring powder or earth-like pigment.

Michaias is a proper name used to identify people in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a personal designation. The name appears 36 times in the Greek Old Testament, across several historical and prophetic books, and is rendered “Michaias” in the available English translation support. Because the same name occurs in different passages, the particular person meant must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage. Its normal function is simply to name an individual.

Neemias is a proper name identifying a person named Neemias. It is not presented here as a general description or action word, but as the personal name used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. The name appears 13 times in this Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Ezra, Nehemiah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being discussed.

This Greek LXX word describes someone who is thoughtful and intelligent—able to understand matters carefully and act with sound judgment. It can function as a noun or adjective, referring either to such a person or to the quality of being intelligent. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs nine times, chiefly in Proverbs and also in Sirach. Its use in wisdom literature presents thoughtful intelligence as a recognizable human quality. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective means “eighth,” identifying something that comes after seven others in an ordered sequence. It describes an eighth day, person, offering, time, or other item, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 44 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion, where it marks position or sequence rather than expressing an independent action or quality. Its exact significance in any passage depends on what is being counted or arranged there.

This word describes something positioned behind another person or thing, or located in the back. It can function as a preposition, showing where something is in relation to something else, or as an adverb, indicating a position behind without separately naming the object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 38 times, so it is a recurring spatial word rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX adverb means “quite” or “utterly,” expressing something in a complete or absolute degree. It strengthens the action or description it modifies, showing that something is fully so rather than partly so. The word occurs five times, all in 2 Maccabees, so its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording. Its central idea remains totality or completeness.

This verb means to transgress or overstep—to cross a boundary by disobeying a command or requirement. It describes movement beyond what is permitted, whether the boundary is expressed as an instruction, duty, or stated limit. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 53 times, showing repeated use for violating what should be honored or obeyed. Its ordinary sense is therefore active and concrete: a person crosses over a defined line rather than remaining within the proper path.

This Greek LXX verb means “throw beside.” It describes an action of casting something alongside another thing, rather than simply throwing it away or toward a distant target. Because it is a verb, it expresses what someone does. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Deuterocanonical material, including passages in 1 Samuel, Psalms, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in each sentence depends on the surrounding wording.

This word means “residency”: the condition of living in a place, especially as a resident rather than as one permanently established there. It is a noun describing a period or status of residence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, showing a recurring term for dwelling or remaining in a place. Its exact emphasis in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “exceedingly glad” or “very joyful.” It describes strong happiness rather than ordinary pleasure, and it functions as an action word—someone becomes or is deeply filled with joy. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Job and once in 3 Maccabees. The exact way that joy is expressed in any one passage depends on its surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains intense gladness.

This adjective describes someone or something as “drowned in the sea.” It presents the person or object in a state resulting from being overcome by seawater, rather than naming an action by itself. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, in 3 Maccabees 6:4. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be described further; its basic meaning remains a description of being drowned in the sea.

This Greek LXX verb means “announce”: to make information known or communicate something openly. It describes the act of reporting or declaring a message rather than the message itself. The word appears five times in the LXX corpus represented here, in four verses of 2 Maccabees and one verse of 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being announced and to whom, but its central idea remains the public communication of information.

This word means “prophet,” referring to a person identified in Scripture by that title. It is a noun used for individual prophets and for prophets as a group. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 305 times, showing that the term is used broadly across historical, prophetic, and other biblical books. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “foal,” referring to a young horse. It names the animal itself rather than an action, quality, or person. The word appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament, across Genesis, Judges, Proverbs, and Zechariah. Its repeated use in these passages shows a consistent reference to a young horse, while the precise significance of the animal in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This adjective describes something that bears or carries roses. It is a descriptive word, so it identifies a person, object, or feature by its association with roses rather than naming the roses themselves. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 7:17. The available meaning is straightforward, but the exact thing it describes in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means a “net” or “seine,” a broad fishing net used to gather fish. It names a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Habakkuk 1:15. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a net used for catching or collecting fish.

Samaa is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twelve times across twelve verses, most often in 1 Chronicles, and also in Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 1 Kings. Because the available meaning is simply the name “Samaa,” its significance cannot be determined from the name alone. The surrounding verse and passage identify which person is meant in each occurrence.

Serouch, also rendered Serukh, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek LXX text. This name occurs five times in the LXX corpus: four times in Genesis 11 and once in 1 Chronicles 1. Its meaning is therefore chiefly its identity as the name of a person, while the surrounding passage determines what is said about that person in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “emerald,” naming a gemstone rather than an action, quality, or person. It identifies the object itself when used in a sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Esther 1:6. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the word’s ordinary meaning can be stated clearly, but its precise role in that verse cannot be described. The central sense remains “emerald.”

This Greek LXX noun refers to dropping or dripping—the falling of liquid in drops. It describes the drops themselves or the act of liquid falling gradually, rather than a broad idea such as flowing or pouring. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 9:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the small, repeated falling of liquid. This Greek LXX verb means “sit together” or “sit in council.” It describes people taking their places together, especially in a gathered setting where they may deliberate or serve as a council. The word occurs four times in the Deuterocanonical books, in Sirach and Susanna, so its normal sense is focused and specific rather than broad. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is simply on sitting together or on participating in a council gathering.

This adjective describes someone or something as “safe” or “unharmed.” It refers to being preserved from injury, danger, or loss, and functions as a description of a person or thing’s condition.
